newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW - New Zealand Budget Policy Statement.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - New Zealand Budget Policy Statement.

text.p: Following are economists' reactions to New Zealand's Budget Policy Statement on Tuesday in which Treasurer Winston Peters reaffirmed the government's prudent fiscal stance.
PAUL STEWART, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK

"Winston Peters and the government are clearly signalling a very strong intention to keep within the parameters that they outlined in the (December) coalition agreement, so that's reasonably reassuring.

"But I think it's important not to lose sight of the fact that there is still a fair degree of fiscal slippage built into the profile over the three-year period, so talk about fiscal prudence, I think, has to be kept in the right sort of context.

"There may be, if anything, slightly less pressure on monetary policy over the next 12 months as a result of the small reduction in expected spending in that year. But it's very marginal -- two or three hundred million dollars is not a lot in the context of overall government spending.

"But it's at least reassuring that there's been no further slippage, that in the near term the increase in government spending is not greater than previously expected. That would have certainly concerned financial markets."

"The Reserve Bank's forecasts will change dramatically from the forecasts in December, not as a result of today's document but as a result of the December 10 Coalition Agreement, specifically, the widening of the inflation target to 0-3 percent, the very large increase in spending this year and in 1998 and 1999 and the rise in the minimum wage rate.
"We think the combined impact of those three things is going to see the Reserve Bank revise up its forecasts quite a lot."
In December the RB was forecasting zero inflation by the end of 1998.
"We suspect the numbers they publish next week will be closer to 1.5 (percent)."

Asked about Peters' comment that there was no room for fiscal easing, Plank said: "I'm not sure what he means there, because he has just gone out and eased fiscal policy massively over the next three years.

"I suppose what he meant is that there is no room for fiscal easing over and above the very large fiscal easing we have already done. I hope he doesn't believe he is being fiscally tight." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
